question.prompt: How many three-digit positive integers \(\underline{a} \ \underline{b} \ \underline{c}\) are there whose nonzero digits \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) satisfy \[0.\overline{\underline{a}~\underline{b}~\underline{c}} = \dfrac{1}{3} (0.\overline{a} + 0.\overline{b} + 0.\overline{c})?\] (The bar indicates digit repetition, thus \(0.\overline{\underline{a}~\underline{b}~\underline{c}}\) is the infinite repeating decimal \(0.\underline{a}~\underline{b}~\underline{c}~\underline{a}~\underline{b}~\underline{c}~\cdots\))

solutions.explanation:
Convert the repeating decimals into fractions so the digits satisfy an ordinary integer equation. For example, \(0.\overline{abc}=(100a+10b+c)/999\), while \(0.\overline a=a/9\). Hence
\[
\frac{100a+10b+c}{999}=\frac{a+b+c}{27}.
\]
Multiplication and simplification give \(7a=3b+4c\). Rewriting the right side as \(3(b-c)+7c\) shows that \(7\) divides \(3(b-c)\). Since \(3\) has no factor \(7\), \(7\) divides \(b-c\).

The digits range from \(1\) to \(9\), so \(-8\le b-c\le8\). Thus \(b-c\) can only be \(-7,0,7\).

If \(b=c\), the equation gives \(a=b=c\), producing \(111,222,\ldots,999\): nine numbers. The other digit pairs are \((b,c)=(1,8),(8,1),(2,9),(9,2)\). Substitution gives \(518,481,629,592\), respectively. Each has a nonzero digit \(a\), so all four count.

The total is \(9+4=\boxed{13}\), choice D. Divisibility plus a narrow digit range turns an algebraic equation into a short complete list.
solutions.title: Convert repeating decimals to fractions and restrict digit differences modulo seven.
